title: Petra and the Language
premise: Xanthe Delacroix has spent three years writing postcards to her childhood home — an address that burned down with everything inside it, including the truth of what happened the night of the fire. When a stranger named Tomas appears at her mother's funeral calling the family by their pre-exile surname, Varga, he drags into the open a history Xanthe has survived by refusing to speak. As the city schedules the burned lot for demolition, Xanthe and Tomas piece together the night her father was taken by men operating outside any law, and discover that her postcards were never going to an empty address at all. To survive what she learns, she must finally say goodbye out loud — naming her father, her old name, and her own guilt — before the bulldozers arrive.
about_author: Cyrus Yarrow is the pen name of a former court interpreter who spent a decade transcribing other people's confessions before writing his own fiction. He lives near a river that changes its name every fifty miles, and writes in the margins of demolition notices.

chapters.title: Poste Restante
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. She buys a postcard at a kiosk, writes to 14 Alder Row, and mails it to a house that burned down years ago. Establishes her ritual, her rented room, her tenant-like existence. Emotional beat: quiet, practiced grief disguised as habit.

chapters.title: The Funeral Weather
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. Her mother's funeral: small turnout, wrong flowers, a eulogy that names no one. Xanthe performs the role of grieving daughter without feeling permitted to grieve. Beat: numbness cracking at the edges.

chapters.title: A Name Nobody Uses
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. A stranger at the graveside says 'Varga' aloud — the family name from before. He introduces himself as Tomas, claims he knew her father. She walks away; he leaves a card with no phone number, only an address. Beat: vertigo.

chapters.title: Fourteen Alder Row
chapters.summary: Tomas's POV. He visits the burned lot, stands where the house stood, and reads the city notice stapled to the fence: demolition in six weeks. Reveals he has been receiving the postcards — forwarded through a dead letter office. Beat: patient resolve.

chapters.title: Tenant, Not Owner
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. Back in her flat, she inventories her life: nothing owned, nothing signed, nothing permanent. A neighbor asks about the funeral and she lies smoothly. Beat: the cost of self-erasure made visible.

chapters.title: The Card That Came Back
chapters.summary: Tomas's POV. He shows Xanthe one of her own postcards, returned undeliverable, then kept. Her handwriting on the back describes a memory only she and her father shared. She realizes someone has been reading her words for years. Beat: exposure.

chapters.title: What the Fire Report Says
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. She requests the official fire report; it lists cause as electrical, occupants as none. But her father died that night, off the record. The state erased him twice. Beat: cold anger arriving late.

chapters.title: Men Without Badges
chapters.summary: Tomas's POV. Flashback chapter: Tomas, then a junior clerk, witnessed plainclothes men take Xanthe's father from his shop — no warrant, no paperwork, justice administered by whoever held the keys. Beat: dread and complicity.

chapters.title: The Interpreter's Silence
chapters.summary: Tomas's POV. Tomas reveals he interpreted during her father's detention hearing and translated the proceedings into language so sanitized the record shows nothing happened. He has come to confess. Beat: shame seeking absolution.

chapters.title: You Were There
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. She refuses his confession — rage, accusation, the charge that his clean sentences helped kill her father. She burns his card in the sink. Beat: grief weaponized.

chapters.title: Demolition Date
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. The city posts the final schedule: the lot comes down in five weeks. She realizes the last physical trace of her father will be legally erased, and no one will object. Beat: countdown begins.

chapters.title: Aunt Riva's Kitchen
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. She visits her aunt, the last relative who uses the old name, hoping for the truth. Riva feeds her, deflects, and finally says only: ask about the ledger. Beat: warmth laced with warning.

chapters.title: The Ledger
chapters.summary: Tomas's POV. Tomas explains the ledger: her father kept accounts of everyone the extralegal men extorted — names, amounts, dates. It vanished the night of the fire. Whoever holds it holds the only evidence. Beat: stakes sharpened.

chapters.title: Someone Is Reading My Mail
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. At the dead letter office, a clerk admits the postcards were redirected — by request — to a private box. She demands the requester's name; the form is signed with her father's handwriting. Beat: uncanny hope.

chapters.title: He Wrote Back Once
chapters.summary: Tomas's POV. Tomas produces a single reply her father smuggled out before his death, addressed to the burned house, knowing Xanthe would write there someday. It says: don't look for me, look for the ledger. Beat: devastating tenderness.

chapters.title: Don't Look for Me
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. She rereads the note all night, furious at his protection, starved for it. She decides to disobey him for the first time in her life. Beat: rebellion born of love.

chapters.title: The Men Still Meet
chapters.summary: Tomas's POV. Surveillance chapter: the men from the old case still gather weekly at a social club, older now, untouchable, respected. One of them, Dorn, signs the demolition permits. Beat: injustice wearing a suit.

chapters.title: An Offer of Help
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. A lawyer named Ilse approaches Xanthe — she represented another victim's family years ago and failed. She offers to help find the ledger, but warns that pursuing it outside the courts means no protection. Beat: alliance formed.

chapters.title: What Survival Cost
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. Midpoint reckoning: Xanthe admits how much of herself she traded to stay safe — the name, the language of her childhood, the right to mourn publicly. She has been surviving instead of living. Beat: painful self-recognition.

chapters.title: Dorn at the Club
chapters.summary: Tomas's POV. Tomas confronts Dorn obliquely, posing as a records researcher. Dorn recognizes him, smiles, and mentions the fire report's tidy conclusion. The threat is polite and total. Beat: fear with a handshake.

chapters.title: The Flat Is Searched
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. Someone enters her flat while she's out — nothing stolen, everything touched. Her postcards are fanned across the bed like dealt cards. Message received. Beat: violation; the past is not passive.

chapters.title: Ilse's Warning
chapters.summary: Ilse's POV. Ilse tells Xanthe about the last family who pushed: they left the country, or worse. Justice outside the law cuts both ways — the men operate there too. Xanthe must choose her battlefield. Beat: the price is named.

chapters.title: Riva Breaks
chapters.summary: Riva's POV. Confronted with the smuggled note, Aunt Riva finally talks: she helped hide the ledger the night of the fire, gave it to a stranger for safekeeping, and has regretted the choice for decades. Beat: confession as relief and wound.

chapters.title: The Stranger Who Kept It
chapters.summary: Tomas's POV. The stranger was a railway worker, long dead — but his daughter still lives in the harbor district and never opened what she was given. Tomas and Xanthe travel to find her. Beat: pilgrimage.

chapters.title: The Harbor District
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. They find Marta, the railway worker's daughter, elderly and suspicious. She has kept a sealed tin for forty years because her father said a Varga would come asking. Beat: faith across generations.

chapters.title: Opening the Tin
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. The tin holds the ledger — and her father's wedding ring, which he was 'not wearing' when he died. Xanthe reads the first page: her own birth recorded in his hand. Beat: overwhelming return of the disowned past.

chapters.title: Names in the Ledger
chapters.summary: Tomas's POV. The ledger names dozens of victims — and, crucially, two of the men who later became city officials, including Dorn's mentor. This is why the record stayed clean. Beat: the machinery of silence exposed.

chapters.title: What Would Justice Look Like
chapters.summary: Xanthe and Tomas debate, alternating POVs. Courts will bury it; publicity endangers them; violence makes them the men they hate. Xanthe decides: the victims' families deserve the truth first, whatever comes after. Beat: moral center chosen.

chapters.title: Letters to the Living
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. She begins writing again — real letters this time, to the families in the ledger, telling them what happened to their people. Each envelope is an act of restitution. Beat: purpose replacing ritual.

chapters.title: Dorn Learns
chapters.summary: Dorn's POV. Dorn discovers copies exist. He offers Xanthe money, then citizenship-clean records, then implies harm. She records nothing, promises nothing, and understands the clock is now measured in days. Beat: menace closing in.

chapters.title: Ilse's Last Case
chapters.summary: Ilse's POV. Ilse files what she can within the law — a complaint, a records petition — knowing it will stall, purely to create a paper trail that protects Xanthe. Justice as shield rather than sword. Beat: dignity in futility.

chapters.title: The Night Before Demolition
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. Eve of destruction. Xanthe sits on the fence of the lot with the ledger in her bag, waiting for the families she wrote to. Some come; some don't. Beat: vigil, community assembling from scattered grief.

chapters.title: Reading at Fourteen Alder Row
chapters.summary: Multiple POVs. At dawn, before the crews arrive, the families read the ledger's pages aloud on the empty lot — each name spoken where the house stood. The dead are witnessed publicly for the first time. Beat: catharsis, communal resurrection.

chapters.title: Dorn Arrives
chapters.summary: Climax part one. Dorn comes to stop the reading; cameras and witnesses hold him frozen. Tomas publicly names himself as the interpreter who sanitized the record, surrendering his safety to break the circle of silence. Beat: courage as contagion.

chapters.title: What the Machines Take
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. The demolition proceeds anyway — but the story is already loose, picked up by a journalist among the families. The building falls; the truth does not. Xanthe watches the walls come down and feels lighter, not bereft. Beat: paradoxical release.

chapters.title: Inquiry
chapters.summary: Epilogue-in-motion. An inquiry opens; Dorn resigns quietly; Tomas testifies and loses his pension and gains his name back. Justice arrives partial, slow, imperfect — but arrives. Beat: sober satisfaction.

chapters.title: Saying Goodbye Properly
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. At the cleared lot, now bare earth, Xanthe speaks aloud to her father — full sentences, his name, her old name, forgiveness she thought she'd never owe. She buries the wedding ring where the kitchen was. Beat: the goodbye the whole book has owed.

chapters.title: Owner of Something
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. She signs a lease — her name, Xanthe Delacroix Varga, both names on one line. First thing she has owned in years is her own identity. She plants something in a pot, not a plot. Beat: quiet reclamation.

chapters.title: The Last Postcard
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. She writes one final postcard to 14 Alder Row, thanks the house for holding her words all these years, and doesn't mail it. She keeps it in a drawer with the ring's box. Some letters are for the living after all. Beat: ritual transformed.

chapters.title: The Language We Keep
chapters.summary: Final chapter, Xanthe's POV. Months later: the inquiry grinds on, some families got settlements, some got only the truth, and the truth was not nothing. Xanthe teaches a neighbor's child the old alphabet. The language survives because someone spoke it out loud. Beat: earned, unglamorous hope.
